title: Post-Tuning Beats Its Own Baseline and Still Loses to a Tuned Rule: LLM Agents from 0.6B to 8B on a Simulated Beer Game

abstract: A published claim reports that RL post-training turns a 4B language model into a cheaper supply-chain agent than the same model untrained [1] (Long, Simchi-Levi, Zhu, Su, Calmon and Calmon, 2026). We test a claim of that type at four sizes (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B) under a pre-registered paired cost criterion, with matched untrained controls. Post-training does help at 4B: 9, 346 against 21, 578, 30/30 paired wins. It does not help at 0.6B, where six trained rows lose and a seventh procedure stops itself; it makes 1.7B worse on every seed (27, 706 to 94, 887 against 11, 508); and at 8B one arm of four passes (14, 594 against 89, 633). The result that survives all of it is simpler: no arm at any size beats the reference we actually care about. A self-tuning order-up-to rule costs 5, 346 on the same 30 demand paths. The best arm is 1.75x that, the worst 17.8x, and the ladder never crosses it. Post-training moves the model within a band far above a 1970s inventory rule; scale did not close the gap.
